FL-052.label: The scoreboard counts right and wrong injection decisions, injected or not, with no arbitrary scoring.
FL-052.walk: Open the scoreboard; it shows separate integer counts of right and wrong decisions (the weighted-disagreement figures are the tuner's trigger, not a score on a memory).
FL-052.observed: Injection Console and Palace State show separate integer Right 0 and Wrong 0, with weighted agreement separately labeled. Verification feedback is excluded from authentic counts.

FL-053.label: Every feature's weight labeled and shown normalized to a decimal.
FL-053.walk: Open the Injection Console; each feature's weight is labeled and shown as a decimal.
FL-053.observed: Injection Console exposes labeled decimal weights: Meaning 0.42, Keywords 0.16, Recency 0.11, Project 0.16, Use count 0.08 and Past choices 0.07; total 1.00.

FL-056.label: Automatic training of the memory line and the share from human feedback, switching on by itself after 100 pieces of authentic feedback.
FL-056.walk: Below 100 pieces of feedback the ledger says the memory line and share are fixed; the 100 floor is shown.
FL-056.observed: The console explicitly states that memory share and injection line stay fixed until 100 authentic signals, with 100 to go.

FL-060.label: An optimization ledger: state and scores across runs in a proper history schema.
FL-060.walk: Force retrain; a row appears in the optimization ledger with its state and score.
FL-060.observed: Pressed FORCE RETRAIN. A fresh insufficient-data entry appeared and the UI reported 0/25 authentic signals. No scored challenger or successful optimization was fabricated.

FL-151.label: KV-cache optimization, usage accounting, and sticky sessions on one provider for cache benefits.
FL-151.walk: Send several messages in one thread; the spend module's KV cache column fills in after the first message and the provider stays the same across the thread.
FL-151.observed: Real OpenRouter messages populated KV cache receipts. The first fixture message showed 1,024 cached tokens and 46.3% reuse; later messages reached 88.9%. Model changes were explicit, not silent provider hopping.

FL-155.label: An append-only spend ledger with fine-grain cost history, its smallest grain a uuid spend unit, and the spend views derived from it.
FL-155.walk: Send one message, then open the spend ledger; new rows with their own uuid spend unit ids appear beneath the unchanged older rows, and the spend module's totals add up from them.
FL-155.observed: Scoped SQL comparison preserved all 114 earlier receipts unchanged and added six uniquely identified lines after another real message. The manual invoice remains exactly one $25.15 row. Current receipt identities are ULIDs, not UUID-formatted strings; the append-only accounting claim is demonstrated.

FL-159.label: The spend module: a row per thread expanding to models, columns input / KV cache / reasoning / output / total / spend per hour, other costs as their own rows, scopable to a thread or stack.
FL-159.walk: Press the plus on one thread row in the spend module; it opens to that thread's models with the columns input, KV cache, reasoning, output, total and spend per hour, with an everything-else row beneath.
FL-159.observed: Expanded the two-model thread: input, KV cache, reasoning, output, total and spend/hour columns appear. Building and Memory keeping remain separate Other work rows beneath the conversations.

FL-197.label: Spend and Palace state reads use the calling principal; only the configured owner can request the whole Palace.
FL-197.walk: In a verification daemon, open Spend and Palace State and see only that principal's receipts and counts. In a local fixture, compare the configured owner's whole-Palace view. Request scope=palace as the verification principal and see a plain 403. Keep owner-rack captures out of evidence.
FL-197.observed: The released app shows only the fresh real-Palace principal's receipts and zero memories; no invoice form is offered. The real scope=palace request returned 403. The separate locally configured fixture owner showed its aggregate spend and invoice form; no real-owner rack was captured.

FL-169.label: Client and cloud versions stay sync-locked or backward compatible, following industry practice, so version differences feel seamless.
FL-169.walk: Start a client whose version differs from the cloud Palace's; it either keeps working or refuses with a plain version message.
FL-169.observed: The public 0.1.16 client doctor accepted Palace API 0.1.18 within its declared >=0.1.0,<0.2.0 range and reported the remote Palace healthy. The public 0.1.18 client also passed.

FL-195.label: The feature ledger generates coverage reports and requires evidence for the rows affected by a build.
FL-195.walk: Compute the composer fix's impact with --paths and see attunement rows; push a branch touching socket.ts and observe the hook print rows and write impacted.json; observe a DONE handoff without screenshots fail CI, then verify complete evidence passes.
FL-195.observed: Ran the current Garden verifier's 30 tests, including impacted-path reporting, missing-evidence DONE refusal and complete-evidence acceptance. Both product impact reports were generated. No deliberately incomplete hosted DONE push was made in this walk; local negative controls do not claim that literal hosted-CI exercise.

FL-196.label: The rules machine checks citations, frozen law, product vocabulary, seed states and packet precedents.
FL-196.walk: Remove a guard citation on a disposable branch and observe CI fail; change a frozen axiom and observe the freeze step fail; restore both and observe Rules pass. The master ADR check remains red until the owner applies the citation patch.
FL-196.observed: Removing A-066 citations in a temporary copy made the checker fail; restoring them passed. The freeze negative-control test and all four final rule checks passed. No deliberately broken disposable branch was sent to hosted CI, so that literal portion remains unproven.

FL-021.label: The memory visualizer shows the hyperparameters and lets the user go in and tweak memories.
FL-021.walk: Open the memory visualizer; the hyperparameters are displayed and a memory can be edited from there.
FL-021.observed: Selected the wool-hat node in Memory Graph, opened Scoring parameters, edited the fictional body to blue wool hat, and saved through the inline editor.

FL-049.label: Scoring parameters that can be added and removed easily; curators can add and retire axes over time.
FL-049.walk: Add or remove a scoring axis in config; the score breakdown gains or loses that row.
FL-049.observed: Inspected Injection Console scoring controls. Existing numeric weights are editable; there is no add/remove-axis control. Structural scoring changes remain M3LL work.

FL-058.label: A standing registry of every trainable parameter; all training loops triggered from one place in the code where their documentation lives.
FL-058.walk: Open the trainable-parameter registry; every trainable parameter is listed, and the training trigger point is one place in code with its documentation beside it.
FL-058.observed: The console lists its current scoring controls and the code registry describes model controls. A complete registry of all trainables and one documented trigger remains unbuilt M3LL work.

FL-059.label: Optimization at every compaction of a main thread, one at a time under a lock, with mixed and capped back-test material.
FL-059.walk: Cross a compaction on a main thread; one optimization runs under a lock on a capped, mixed back-test.
FL-059.observed: Main-thread compaction ran on the disposable principal. The console excludes its verification signals, and force retrain returned insufficient_data at 0/25. This does not prove a successful scored optimization or challenger adoption.

FL-162.label: Easy onboarding from a single splash repo, needing only two secrets: a GCP credential and an OpenRouter key.
FL-162.walk: On a fresh machine, follow the splash repo's install steps; you are asked for a GCP credential and an OpenRouter key and nothing else before the app comes up.
FL-162.observed: Installed and reinstalled the public wheels in clean disposable environments on this Mac. This is not a literal fresh-machine two-credential onboarding or new GCP provisioning walk.
